findings.title: Denial cache key is ambiguous: name/parent concatenation can collide
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` builds the key as `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`. Because `_` is a legal character in Grafana resource/folder UIDs, different (name, parent) pairs map to the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="c" and name="a", parent="b_c" both yield `...action_a_b_c`. Since `Check` now short-circuits to `Allowed: false` on any hit in this cache (service.go:117), a denial recorded for one resource can silently deny access to a completely different resource the user is actually permitted to see, for up to the 30s TTL. Use an unambiguous encoding (e.g. length-prefixed or a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions, or hash the tuple).

findings.title: Every denied Check now triggers a full permission re-query from the DB
findings.body: The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions` and `Check` now only returns early from the cache when the cached scope map *allows* the request. Any request that is not allowed by the cached permissions falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which always queries the permission store. Combined with a denial cache that is keyed per (action, name, parentFolder), this means every distinct resource a user is denied on causes a fresh DB round-trip (user permissions, and on a cold cache basic roles and teams) once per 30s TTL window. Deny-heavy workloads (UI browsing/filtering that issues many per-resource Checks) will see a large increase in authz DB queries compared to before this change. Consider bounding the re-query (e.g. only re-query if the permission cache entry is older than some threshold, or a short negative-result TTL on the permission fetch itself).

findings.title: Denial is cached even when it is caused by a stale folder tree
findings.body: The fallback path re-queries permissions from the database, but `checkPermission` -> `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still uses `folderCache` (30s TTL). If a folder was just created/moved and is missing from the cached tree, the inherited-permission check fails and the resulting denial is then written into `permDenialCache` for another 30s. So a denial caused purely by a stale folder tree gets pinned for up to ~2x the folder cache TTL, and the problem this PR is meant to fix (access to just-created folders/dashboards) still reproduces for resources whose access is inherited through a newly created folder. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the (possibly stale) folder tree, or refresh/bypass the folder cache on the fallback path.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric no longer measures cache hit rate
findings.body: `permissionCacheUsage` is incremented with "true" only when the cached permissions allow the request, and the unconditional `WithLabelValues("false", ...)` at this line is also reached when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` *succeeded* but the decision was deny. A permission-cache hit that results in a deny is therefore reported as a cache miss. In addition, a hit in the new `permDenialCache` (line 118) is reported as a `permissionCacheUsage` hit, conflating two different caches. The metric no longer reflects the permission cache hit rate, which makes it useless for tuning TTLs and for detecting cache regressions; it should either count hits/misses of the permission cache independently of the decision, or use a separate label/metric for the denial cache.

findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually prove the short-circuit
findings.body: The subtest "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" comments "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked" but seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, i.e. the scope map does *not* grant access. With or without the `permDenialCache` entry the request would be denied (the default fake store returns no permissions), so the test passes even if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed. Set the scope to `true` so the test fails if the denial cache is not consulted, and additionally assert that the store was not queried (e.g. `fakeStore.calls == 0`).

findings.title: In-proc authz client loses all client-side result caching
findings.body: Replacing the authlib local cache with `NoopCache` for the in-proc client means every `Check` and every `Compile`/List performed by API handlers now goes through the in-proc gRPC channel and is fully re-evaluated server-side on every request; previously results were cached for 30s on the client. Server-side caching only covers the raw permission/identity lookups, not the per-request work: building the allowed folder/item sets in `listPermission` walks the whole scope map and folder subtree on every call, and (per the server change) any denied Check falls through to a DB query. For instances with many permissions/folders this is a noticeable per-request CPU and DB cost increase. If the goal is only freshness for newly created resources, consider a very short client TTL rather than disabling the cache entirely.
